text: of calcineurin inhibitors have been investigated; improved renal function has been re- ported, but use of sirolimus may increase the risk of coro- nary artery disease, and long-term results are lack- ing.17,37,38 Although newer drugs have decreased the incidence of acute rejection, there is only limited evidence that this has improved longer-term graft survival.39-41 The one-year cadaveric graft survival is about 88% and about 60% at 10 years.42 Recurrence of the original disease or de novo renal disease may also cause graft failure.43 Pentoxifylline44 and gusperimus45 may improve graft survival. Cardiovascular disease is a major cause of death in renal transplant patients.46 Corticosteroids and ciclosporin can impair endothelial function, cause hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia. Sirolimus has also been implicated in hyperlipidaemia.46 Dyslipidaemia occurs in about 60% of patients after renal transplantation;12,46 HMG-CoA reduct- ase inhibitors (statins) and dietary modification have been recommended as first-line treatment by some,12 whereas others47 recommend drug treatment with various lipid- lowering drugs only if lifestyle changes are insufficient. Modification of the immunosuppressive protocols, as dis- cussed above, may also be effective.12 Hyperuricaemia is a common problem among renal trans- plant recipients;48 the use of ciclosporin is an independent risk factor for new-onset gout after transplantation.49 Use of sirolimus is also associated with an increased risk, whereas use of tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil car- ries a lower risk. Hyperuricaemia, besides having direct deleterious effects on the graft, may potentiate chronic re- nal dysfunction induced by calcineurin inhibitors, and con- tribute to chronic allograft nephropathy.48 New-onset gout after transplantation may also be associated with hyperten- sion, cardiovascular disease, and death.49 Morbidity and mortality have improved with reductions in cardiac, vascular and infectious complications, but there has been no decrease in death from malignancy, and the risk of developing cancer has been estimated to be about 100% by 30 years post-transplant.50 Compared with the general population, renal transplant recipients have a three- to fivefold higher risk of malignancy; cancers tend to be more aggressive in transplant recipients, and solid or- gan tumours have a poorer prognosis. The most common malignancies include non-melanoma skin cancers and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD).51,52 While not all malignancies are a consequence of transplan- tation or immunosuppressive therapy,51 both the duration and intensity of immunosuppression have been linked to this increased incidence.52 Other risk factors include in- creasing age, male gender,53 sun exposure, and cigarette smoking.51 It is difficult to assess the impact of individual drugs on cancer risk;51
